items.title: Announcing the retirement of R and Python visuals in Power BI
items.excerpt: The built-in R and Python visuals in Power BI will retire in May 2027 . What changes This retirement applies only to R and Python visuals in interactive Power BI reports. Python scripts used in Power Query to populate tables are not affected. Power BI service: At retirement, all R and Python visuals will stop working in published reports, including those published before retirement. R-powered custom visuals: Custom visuals that use R will also no longer work at retirement. Older versions of Power BI Desktop: These visuals will continue to work locally using R and Python installed on your machine. Future versions of Power BI Desktop: After retirement, R and Python visuals will be removed, so you won't be able to add them to reports. What you need to do No migration within your report will recreate your exact R or Python visual. You must replace it with a different visualization before retirement. Start reviewing your reports for R and Python visuals and communicate within your organization that reports using them will be impacted. Preserve their scripts and dependencies. items.excerpt: Building and operating a data warehouse is increasingly a software engineering discipline. Teams want to develop warehouse changes in isolation, version them in Git, review them through pull requests, promote them safely across environments, and automate the entire process using their existing CI/CD systems. Over the past several releases, we've been evolving CI/CD in Fabric Warehouse around that lifecycle: DacFx established a common schema deployment foundation. Pre, and post-deployment scripts expanded deployments beyond schema changes. Warehouse Item Definition APIs opened the same lifecycle to automation. Together, these investments are creating a more complete CI/CD lifecycle for Fabric Warehouse, from developing and versioning database changes to deploying and automating them across environments. Let’s take a closer look at how each capability moves that experience forward, what’s available today, and what we’re building next. items.title: OneLake table APIs: Now with Iceberg writes, plus richer table metadata (Preview)
items.excerpt: OneLake table APIs already let Iceberg-compatible engines discover and read tables in Microsoft Fabric. Today we're taking the next step with two additions: Iceberg REST Catalog (IRC) writes through the OneLake table endpoint, now available, and a new additional table metadata API, in preview, for adding descriptions and tags to tables and columns. Together, they make OneLake a place where any engine can not only read data, but also publish it, with the business context people and AI agents need to use it well. Write native Iceberg tables from the engines you already use Until now, the OneLake Iceberg endpoint supported read-only metadata operations. Now, IRC-compatible clients can create native Iceberg tables, commit new snapshots, and request short-lived storage credentials through the same endpoint they already use for reads. That means engines such as PyIceberg, Snowflake, and DuckDB can land results directly in OneLake using standard Iceberg tooling, with no custom connectors or copy jobs. items.title: Regular expression functions in Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse (Preview)
items.excerpt: Data warehouses routinely ingest valuable information embedded in free text, where inconsistent structure makes it difficult to query, connect, and analyze. Incoming values can also require quality checks before they reach curated tables. Microsoft Fabric Data Warehouse and the SQL analytics endpoint now support scalar regular expression functions in preview, so you can extract useful values, validate formats, standardize text, and mask sensitive data directly in T-SQL instead of adding a separate processing step. What’s new in preview Regular expressions provide a concise way to recognize, extract, and transform complex text patterns that would otherwise require multiple string operations. The preview introduces the following scalar functions: REGEXP_LIKE : checks whether text matches a pattern. REGEXP_REPLACE : replaces matching text to clean, standardize, or mask values. REGEXP_SUBSTR : extracts a substring that matches a pattern. REGEXP_INSTR : returns the position of a matching substring. REGEXP_COUNT : counts pattern occurrences in a string. Yet environment-specific connection details and destination references can make each release a manual, error-prone task. Variable library integration with Eventstream in Microsoft Fabric lets teams reuse the same eventstream definition across environments, with references that resolve to each environment's resources. What's new? Variable library integration with Eventstream is available in preview. For supported source connections and destination items, you can use variable library references instead of direct values. These references are preserved through Git integration and deployment pipelines, helping teams reuse an eventstream definition across workspaces with environment-specific configuration. How variable library integration works Variable library is an item type in Microsoft Fabric that provides a centralized way to define and manage configuration values at the workspace level. items.title: Bringing Rust-native Spark compatibility to Microsoft OneLake with Sail and LakeSail
items.excerpt: Coauthor: Shehab Amin Microsoft OneLake gives every Microsoft Fabric tenant a single, unified data lake built on open formats. One copy of data, many engines: that is the promise, and it is what makes OneLake such a strong foundation for analytics and AI alike. This post looks at how Sail , the open-source distributed compute framework, and LakeSail Cloud , the managed platform for running Sail in production, connect natively to OneLake, and what that unlocks for teams running Spark and Python workloads on Fabric. Sail is a drop-in replacement for Apache Spark, rebuilt from the ground up in Rust, with Rust-native support for Delta Lake and Apache Iceberg out of the box. That makes it a natural fit for OneLake, where lakehouse tables are stored in exactly these open formats. Point Sail at a Fabric lakehouse and it reads and writes the same tables the rest of Fabric uses, with no data copies, no extra connectors to install, and no changes to existing Spark code. One engine for data and AI Sail implements the Spark Connect protocol, the gRPC interface that decouples Spark clients from the engine that executes their plans. Existing Spark SQL and DataFrame code targeting Spark 3.5 or 4.

items.title: OneLake: The file system for agent-first data engineering
items.excerpt: Software engineers are increasingly using agents to build software, and data engineers are no different. We want OneLake to help enable data engineers to develop software in this new agent-first era. Think about how you work in a terminal: you use it to run programs that read and write files. Both the programs and the data live in the file system. Now apply that model to data engineering: OneLake is the file system, Fabric engines are the programs, and the AI prompt is your terminal. Over the last few weeks, we’ve released several new capabilities in OneLake that come together to create an experience where agent-first data engineers can thrive. This blog post provides a rundown of those features. Managing OneLake OneLake now offers a remotely hosted MCP server (preview), so agents can explore and manage your data without installing a local server. The local MCP option remains available if you prefer. We’ve also added tools to the Fabric Core MCP server for managing shortcuts and OneLake security . items.excerpt: Co-author: Abhishek Narain Protect continuity, understand connection risk, and set tenant-wide guardrails Imagine that the person who built a business-critical pipeline has left your organization. The connection still exists, but nobody is sure who can manage it or whether its credentials will keep working. What begins as a handover problem quickly becomes a governance question: who owns your connections, where do they lead, and which identities should be allowed to use them? Microsoft Fabric brings these questions together through two complementary capabilities: Admin connection APIs give tenant administrators visibility and ownership-management tools across connection types. Data connection policies set preventive controls for cloud connections. Together, they support a practical sequence: restore responsibility, understand your connections, then enforce the authentication boundaries your organization needs. From recovery to prevention Keep work moving when a connection owner leaves A departure should not leave a connection without someone who can maintain it. items.title: Share data and context across organizations with IQ Share (Preview)
items.excerpt: The data needed to answer a business question rarely belongs to one organization. Enterprises depend on suppliers, software providers, research partners, and customers for information that complement their own. Yet getting that data into their workflow often means building another pipeline, maintaining another copy, and reconciling access across organizational boundaries. Even when the data arrives, its meaning can be left behind. Definitions, assumptions, and usage guidance are shared separately, leaving teams to reconstruct the context before they can put the data to work. With IQ Share in Microsoft Fabric, now in preview, organizations can share supported Fabric data items, along with context stored in lakehouse files, with recipients in other Fabric tenants. Data stays in the producer's tenant, recipients work in their own Fabric workspace, and producers retain control over access. Introducing IQ Share IQ Share brings cross-tenant data and context sharing into a Fabric item-based experience.
